title: Client ergonomics and safety spec for hybrid streaming-pull model
creator: Sofia Martinez
description:
Summary:
This PRD defines a cross-language contract and ergonomic guidance for a hybrid streaming-pull client surface: a streaming API that can be paused and resumed using opaque continuation tokens, while also allowing paginated pull semantics for bulk consumption. The goal is to enable low-latency interactive streaming for front-line features while preserving deterministic retry and migration paths for long-running background jobs that need to resume from checkpoints.

Scope and motivation:
- Languages: Python (async-first), TypeScript (browser/node), Go (context + channels).
- Surface areas: streaming pulls, cursorized pagination, retry semantics, token canonicalization, client-side backpressure signals, cancellation, and migration compatibility across SDK versions.
- Non-goals: server-side storage of long-term checkpoints (we rely on continuation tokens and short expiry), full transactional semantics across multi-request jobs.

Key constraints and design principles:
1) Single durable continuation token per logical stream page. Tokens must be opaque strings (base64) and deterministic for idempotency checking but treated as opaque by clients.
2) Language idioms: Python exposes an async iterator with .resume(token) overload; TS uses async generators/ReadableStream wrappers; Go exposes a StreamPull(ctx) that returns (<-chan Message, ResumeToken) or a small iterator abstraction.
3) Retry safety: Streams must expose per-message idempotency metadata. Clients may retry transient network failures using exponential backoff but must not reapply non-idempotent downstream effects without explicit idempotency keys.
4) Backpressure: Clients can request window_size N; runtime must respect and not exceed window. SDKs should expose a default conservative window and allow override.
5) Token expiry: Tokens expire after 24 hours by default. SDKs should surface expiry errors with guidance to restart from nearest saved checkpoint.
6) Compatibility: New SDK versions must be able to read older tokens for at least two major releases. Server may advertise token version in token metadata.

Deliverables:
- PRD and language-specific guidelines (this doc).
- Test matrix and interoperability harness (cross-language).
- Type-level API proposals for Python/TS/Go and migration guide.
- Acceptance criteria and QA plan.

acceptance_criteria: API contract defined: method names and signatures for Python/TS/Go documented and approved by DX and Lang leads
End-to-end interop test: Python client can start stream, receive 1,000 messages, persist token at 500, resume on a new process and continue to 1000 with message idempotency preserved
Failure modes covered: transient network drop, server-side short outage, token-expiry path all produce deterministic, documented behavior
Retry semantics: SDKs implement default exponential backoff + jitter and a single application-level idempotency header for non-idempotent operations
Backpressure respected: SDKs expose window_size and runtime metrics show no window overruns in integration test
Documentation: language guides, migration notes, and code examples (Py/TS/Go) published to docs.redwood.ai
Observability: stream-level tracing and token change events emitted to console traces and runtime dashboards
Backward compatibility: server-encoded token versioning allows at least two major SDK versions to resume tokens
test_plan: Unit tests for token encoding/decoding (server + SDK shims) in each language
Integration harness: cross-language runner that exercises start/pause/resume cycles under packet loss simulation
Chaos test: simulate server restart and verify client resume semantics and no-duplicate-delivery guarantees where idempotency metadata applied
Performance: measure median and p99 latency for streaming pulls at window sizes [1,8,32] and ensure latency SLOs met
Compatibility matrix: run resume tests with token versions v1..v3 across SDK snapshots
rollout_plan: Cut a compatibility-first beta: release SDK shims with a feature flag for beta customers
Collect telemetry for 2 weeks and run interop tests against production staging runtime
Gradual ramp: enable default behavior for 10% -> 50% -> 100% of requests over 4 weeks, with automatic rollback on error-rate spike
Provide migration guide for customers persisting tokens longer than 24h
lang_guidance_typescript:
API shape (node/browser): const stream = client.streamGenerate(prompt, {windowSize: 8, resumeToken}); for await (const chunk of stream) { /* chunk.id, chunk.text, chunk.meta.resumeToken */ }
Design notes: provide ReadableStream wrapper for browser consumption and an async generator for node. Expose cancel() to close early and return last resume token.
lang_guidance_go:
API shape: ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(ctx) ; msgs, info := client.StreamPull(ctx, req) ; for m := range msgs { /* m.ID, m.Data, info.ResumeToken */ }
Design notes: integrate with context cancellation, return a small iterator helper with Next() (bool) and Err() patterns; avoid goroutine leaks and document recommended buffer sizes.
migration_guide:
- Older clients: server will emit token_version in token payload. New SDKs must accept tokens with version fields but continue to issue v3 tokens when safe.
- Deprecation: v1 tokens will be accepted for 2 major releases after v3 rollout.
- For customers storing tokens beyond expiry, recommend periodic checkpointing and include token timestamp metadata.
open_questions: Should the runtime support long-lived server-side checkpoints for enterprise customers? (security/ops trade-offs)
What is the canonical field name for idempotency metadata across models (message_id vs sequence_id)?
Agree timeout semantics for typed SDK methods: should default client-level timeout be 5 minutes or configurable per-stream?

2026-03-08: Security reviewed token expiry; recommended default 24h with enterprise override behind feature flag.
